_note: Every number here was measured; the result file is named next to it. Update after re-running a benchmark, then rebuild both documents.
u1: learned from 300 live lines without a restart; >= 99 % of the next 1,000 lines parsed by it; in defence mode 0 events used it before approval
u2: 5,000 events in 5 seals; an edited column, a nulled MAC and a rewritten hash each located at the exact record
u5: a vendor field rename gives 1 drift event within 1,000 lines; a 5-step kill chain across 2 inputs gives 1 correlation group
onboarding: a 200-line sample becomes an active parser in 0.15 s, with 100 % coverage
performance: 3 workers, industry defaults (journal, seals, drift, anomaly, correlation)
2 nodes x 3 workers on the same 4-core host
Soak: 60 min at 5,000 ev/s, 7 workers, 18,000,000 events
Single core, parse + normalise + enrich only
sizing: One billion events a day is about 11,600 events/s on average. One 6-worker node on this laptop persisted 26,952 events/s, about 2.3 billion a day. Nodes share nothing on the data path, so capacity adds per node. Plan nodes at about 60 % of the rate measured on the target hardware, to leave headroom for bursts and post-outage drains. The embedded DuckDB store's memory grows with stored rows, so at sustained high volume keep it for a retention window and send bulk data to the Parquet lake or a SIEM.
coverage: Every source class (network devices, servers and OS, applications, databases, cloud, containers, EDR, IAM, IoT, hardware) and every expected solution a–k has an implementation and a test; see docs/PROBLEM_STATEMENT_COVERAGE.md. Open: the Kafka and Event Hubs connectors are config-validated only (no broker or SDK available), the competitive comparison was not run (Vector, Logstash and Fluent Bit are not installed), and the throughput figures come from a laptop, so server sizing must be measured on the target hardware.
